The objective of this study was to determine if a readily available anion gap (AG) could be used as a surrogate marker for abnormal lactate level in Emergency Department (ED) patients at risk for sepsis. The initial basic chemistry panels, calculated AG, and lactate levels drawn in the ED were collected. **Conclusion:**  This study suggests that an elevated AG obtained in the ED is a moderately sensitive and specific means to detect elevated lactate levels in ED patients at risk for sepsis.

There was poor discriminative performance of the anion gap to predict serum lactate >2 mmol/L (area under ROC is 0.65; 95%CI 0.58-0.72). **Conclusion:** An anion gap >12 mmol/L is not suitable for assessing lactate >2 mmol/L; however, an anion gap >18 mmol/L can predict serum lactate >4 mmol/L in patients with sepsis who had mean arterial pressure (MAP) >65 mmHg. anion gap, sepsis, septic shock, serum lactate.
